title: Modeling of train-induced environmental vibrations from railway traffic: a state-of-the-art review
abstract: Abstract The growing demand for sustainable transport has led to increasing interest in developing rail transit networks for both intra-city and inter-city travel. However, train-induced vibrations may cause significant negative environmental impacts on nearby buildings, sensitive equipment, and residents, thereby garnering considerable attention from researchers and engineers. An efficient prediction model is essential for assessing train-induced vibrations and for designing appropriate vibration mitigation measures. The complex dynamics of the train, track, infrastructure, soils, and buildings, along with their interactions, make the modeling of train-induced environmental vibrations a challenging task. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the current state-of-the-art methods for modeling train-induced vibrations from surface and underground railway traffic. It begins by addressing wave propagation in natural soils, followed by an in-depth examination of analytical, numerical, and empirical approaches for predicting train-induced vibrations in the ground and buildings. Finally, this paper identifies unresolved issues in the field and outlines areas that require further investigation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Railway transportation represents one of the most advanced and fast-developing forms of transport, owing to its efficiency, energy conservation, safety, and comfort. Rail transit networks for both intra-city and inter-city travel are expanding at an accelerated rate worldwide. As shown in Fig.  1 , by the end of 2024, China has opened a total of 162,000 km of railway operating mileage, which includes 48,000 km of high-speed railway. In addition, 58 cities in China have started the urban rail transit operations, with a total mileage of 12,161 km. The expansion of railway networks has a positive effect for reducing congestion, air pollution and greenhouse gases. Fig. 1 Operation mileages of  a  high-speed railways and  b  urban rail transits over years

However, the increasing number of operational railway lines has raised significant environmental concerns, particularly regarding train-induced vibrations. Although these vibrations typically exhibit low amplitudes and do not directly cause structural damage to buildings [ 1 ], they may still lead to long-term structural deterioration, interfere with precision instruments, and disrupt human comfort. A compelling case is the 1000-year-old Probhutaratna Pagoda in Beijing, located just 130 m from a major railway. Although measured vibration levels remained within regulatory thresholds, field studies reported signs of vibration-induced degradation, suggesting that even low-amplitude vibrations can pose long-term risks to historical masonry [ 2 ]. Similarly, in Xi’an, China, the 632-year-old Bell Tower experienced measurable vibration impacts from two spatially overlapping metro lines [ 3 ]. The study revealed that despite mitigation measures like steel spring floating slab tracks and speed restrictions, metro operations contributed to cumulative vibration effects on the ancient timber structure. Additionally, in Peking University laboratories, vibrations from Metro Line 4 caused visible image distortion in electron microscopes, impairing the accuracy of scientific measurements [ 4 ]. For human perspective, vibrations in the frequency range of 1–80 Hz can be perceived by the human body, while those in 16 to 250 Hz can cause acoustic radiation, resulting in rumbling noises audible to building occupants.

Vibrations originate at the wheel/rail interface (Fig.  2 ), where dynamic forces from wheel/rail irregularities and quasi-static forces from rolling wheels jointly excite track vibrations. These vibrations then propagate through ground from surface and underground railways propagate to the nearby buildings. Given the inhomogeneity and strong spatial variability of natural soils, the propagation characteristics of railway-induced vibrations are highly complex. Understanding these vibrations necessitates knowledge of wheel–rail dynamic interactions, soil dynamics, soil–structure interaction, and structural dynamics. Fig. 2 Generation and propagation of railway-induced environmental vibrations

This paper provides a detailed review of methodologies for modeling ground and building vibrations induced by railway traffic. It is organized as follows: Sect.  2  discusses wave propagation in natural soils, while Sects.  3  and  4  focus on the numerical and analytical modeling of ground and building vibrations induced by surface and underground railway traffic, respectively. Section  5  examines empirical and semi-empirical methods. Finally, Sect.  6  offers a discussion on areas for future research.

sections.heading: Wave propagation in natural soils
paragraphs: The waves generated by train operations are three-dimensional in nature, and their attenuation is governed not only by the physical properties of the medium and the distance from the source, but also by factors of the soil such as stratification, inhomogeneity, and anisotropy. This section provides an overview of wave propagation in homogeneous elastic media and wave field generated by moving loads. In addition, the modeling of wave propagation in stratified soils along with the effect of multi-phase and anisotropy is subsequently discussed.

sections.heading: Wave propagation in homogeneous media
paragraphs: The simplest case of wave propagation occurs in an infinite or semi-infinite homogeneous and isotropic medium. This scenario has been extensively studied, dating back to the pioneering works of Stokes, Rayleigh, and Lamb [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 ,  8 – 9 ].

To better understand the energy transmission of different wave types, Gutowski and Dym [ 12 ] compared the energy transfer through a small rigid disk vibrating on a free surface. The results revealed that the Rayleigh waves accounted for the majority of the energy transmission, carrying approximately 67% of the input energy. Both the horizontal and vertical amplitudes of the Rayleigh wave decayed exponentially with increasing distance from the surface. In contrast, S waves and P waves accounted for around 26% and 7% of the input energy, respectively. The amplitude of both body waves diminished as they propagated farther from the source. In addition, the dynamic stress in a homogeneous half-space generated by a point load was investigated [ 13 ]. The results demonstrated that the dynamic effect cannot be ignored in the medium to high frequencies range, where the boundary frequencies are determined by the ratio of actual to nominal shear wave velocity.

sections.heading: Wave field generated by moving loads
paragraphs: When a moving load acts on the ground, resonance occurs when the velocity of the load matches the characteristic wave velocities of the medium. This condition is referred to as the “critical speed”. The dynamic amplification effects associated with critical speed have been studied for over a century [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ]. It is well established that the phenomena of critical speed in a homogeneous half-space can be analyzed within the framework of wave propagation theory.

In the case of a homogeneous medium with non-dispersive waves, moving-load problems can be categorized into three distinct stages, depending on whether the load speed is less than, equal to, or greater than its Rayleigh-wave velocity [ 19 ]. Figure  3  shows the vertical displacement field on the surface of a half-space with a Rayleigh wave velocity of  c R  = 81.4 m/s due to a unit moving load with velocities of  c  = 40, 80, and 100 m/s, as calculated by a thin-layer method (TLM) [ 20 ]. Fig. 3 Vertical displacement field on the surface of a half-space with a Rayleigh wave velocity of  c R  = 81.4 m/s induced by a unit moving load with  a c  = 40 m/s,  b c  = 80 m/s, and  c c  = 100 m/s When the load velocity is below the Rayleigh wave velocity, as illustrated in Fig.  3 a, no propagating waves are generated. In this case, the displacement field behaves similarly to a static load moving over the surface, which is commonly referred to as the “quasi-static problem”. As the load velocity approaches the Rayleigh wave velocity, as illustrated in Fig.  3 b, the wave field transitions, and the dynamic effects begin to dominate the responses. At this point, the displacement field is observable at greater distances, and a small ‘bow wave’ forms at the load position. When the load speed exceeds the Rayleigh wave velocity, as illustrated in Fig.  3 c, propagating waves with significant amplitude are observed, traveling away from the load. This results in large dynamic effects, including the development of a Mach cone.

The physical phenomenon associated with the critical speed is well understood in the context of wave propagation in the homogeneous half-space. However, practical engineering applications demand a more comprehensive understanding of how geotechnical factors, such as soil stratification, inhomogeneity, and anisotropic properties, influence this phenomenon.

Building upon the analysis of surface moving loads, a similar critical speed phenomenon can be observed in underground moving loads, though the wave propagation mechanisms are more complex due to the heterogeneous nature of the medium. In these cases, the load speed relative to the soil’s characteristic wave velocities determines the following [ 17 ]: Subsonic ( c  < shear wave velocity  c s ): The load moves at a speed below the shear wave velocity of the soil. This results in a quasi-static effect, where the vibration field shows exponential decay over distance, similar to surface load behavior. Transonic ( c s  <  c  < compressional wave velocity  c p ): As the load speed approaches the shear wave velocity but remains below the compressional wave velocity, dynamic amplification occurs, and the vibration pattern changes noticeably. Supersonic ( c  >  c p ): When the load speed exceeds the compressional wave velocity, significant dynamic effects are observed, leading to sharp wavefronts and delta-function singularities in the displacement and stress fields.

Furthermore, the presence of soil stratification introduces additional complexity to the wave propagation process in underground loads. Cutoff frequencies—below which waves cannot propagate—adds an additional layer of complexity. For example, Yang et al. [ 21 ] demonstrated that vibrations below 1.2 Hz cannot propagate in a 30 m thick soil layer, which significantly influences vibration behavior.

While surface and underground loads exhibit similar critical speed effects, underground loads are influenced more by soil stratification, which introduces complexity in wave propagation. Unlike surface loads, which exhibit relatively uniform vibration decay with distance, underground loads show significant localized effects, particularly at low frequencies. Additionally, the interaction between soil layers and the presence of cutoff frequencies in layered soils require specialized analysis for wave propagation induced by underground moving loads.

sections.heading: Wave propagation in stratified soils
paragraphs: Natural soils typically consist of multiple layers with varying physical properties. When body waves (P and S waves) encounter an interface between layers, wave reflections, refractions, and conversions occur, resulting in a complex wave field in stratified soils. As illustrated in Fig.  4 , a portion of the incident waves is reflected back into the upper layer, while another portion is refracted into the lower layer. In this context, each layer can be characterized by body waves and surface waves in layered media are generally dispersive in nature. Previous research [ 22 ] indicated that the amplitude of the reflected and refracted waves at the free surface is influenced by material properties, incidence and reflection/refraction angles, and the mechanical impedance of soil layers. Notably, Love waves can be generated when a soft surficial layer overlies a stiffer layer, arising from the interference of trapped S waves within the soft layer, characterized by horizontal transverse particle motion. Fig. 4 A diagram of wave propagation in stratified soils

Various approaches have been developed to model wave propagation in stratified soils. One widely used method is the Thomson–Haskell propagator matrix method (PMM) [ 23 ,  24 ]. This method establishes the relationship between single and multiple layers, calculating the displacement vector from interface to interface using the chain rule. While this method is straightforward and free from additional boundary condition assumptions, it is limited by issues related to numerical overflow and precision loss, particularly under high-frequency excitation and with thicker layers.

Several extensions to the Thomson–Haskell method have been proposed to address these limitations, including the delta matrix method [ 25 ] and reduced delta matrix method [ 26 ]. These extensions may involve an artificial upper limitation of layer thickness, which increases computational cost. Thrower [ 27 ] and Watson [ 28 ] have made further improvements to computational efficiency. Another notable extension is the transmission and reflection matrix (TRM) method, proposed by Fuchs and Müller [ 29 ] as well as Kennett and Kerry [ 30 ,  31 ]. The TRM method uses a recursive algorithm based on the transmission and reflection coefficient matrix, effectively avoiding the complications associated with both positive and negative exponential terms. Therefore, the method offers a simple, flexible implementation that guarantees high numerical accuracy and calculation stability. Luco and Apsel [ 32 ,  33 ] combined the TRM method with the wavenumber integration approach to further enhance its capabilities. In addition, the orthogonalization method proposed by Wang [ 34 ] extends both the matrix method and numerical integration for general use. By inserting an additional procedure into the propagation loop, this method resolves the numerical difficulty inherent in the original Thomson-Haskell propagator algorithm and ensures that all fundamental vectors are orthonormal throughout the computation.

An alternative approach for simulating wave propagation in multi-layered media is the stiffness matrix method (SMM), first proposed by Kausel and Roësset [ 35 ]. This method follows an implementation approach analogous to the finite element method, constructing the system stiffness matrix by assembling individual layer stiffness matrices. Unlike other computational tools, the SMM accurately treats wave propagation without requiring the subdivision of homogeneous layers. As a result, the layers can have arbitrarily thickness, and the method is capable of capturing temporal characteristics of the source at high frequencies [ 36 ,  37 ]. However, the size of the global stiffness matrix increases as the number of layers increases, resulting in low computational efficiency. In addition, to calculate the 3D dynamic responses of layered soils in the space domain, double discrete Fourier transforms of spatial coordinates are required for both the PMM and SMM, which requires an amount of computational cost.

The thin-layer method (TLM), initially introduced by Lysmer and Waas [ 38 ] and later refined by Kausel [ 39 ,  40 – 41 ], provides another choice for simulating wave propagation in layered media. The TLM transforms the complex wave equation into a quadratic characteristic equation through vertical discretization, allowing for the efficient derivation of closed-form solution for displacement fields via modal superposition in the space domain. This eliminates the need of double discrete Fourier transforms, significantly improving computational efficiency compared to the PMM and SMM. The TLM has been widely adopted in elastodynamic problems in geophysics [ 42 ,  43 – 44 ]. Building on the concept of infinite-length thin-layer elements, Kausel and Roësset [ 45 ] proposed a framework of 2D semi-infinite and finite-length thin-layer elements. He et al. [ 46 ] expanded this methodology to 3D applications, enabling more comprehensive modeling of dynamic responses in stratified media with irregular interfaces. The 3D finite-length thin-layer elements can have arbitrary length, independent of frequencies. This characteristic ensures that the length of this element is not limited by the wavelength criterion typically encountered in traditional mesh method such as the finite element method. Nevertheless, the TLM is restricted to media of finite depth. Barbosa et al. [ 47 ] combined the TLM with the PML to investigate dynamic responses of an isotropic layered half-space, exhibiting high efficiency.

sections.heading: The influence of multi-phase and anisotropy
paragraphs: Wave propagation in saturated soils can be analyzed from a macroscopic perspective by modeling soils as a two-phase medium, comprising a solid skeleton and fluid. The dynamics of each phase and the overall mixture can be described using the principles of continuum mechanics, as established by Frenkel [ 48 ] and Biot [ 49 ,  50 ]. Numerous studies have focused on deriving fundamental solution for a layered saturated porous half-space under various dynamic sources and investigating the effect of saturated porous characteristic [ 51 ,  52 ,  53 ,  54 – 55 ]. More complicated models accounted for the existence of a gas phase, resulting in the generation of the P3 waves, which has a non-negligible influence on wave propagation in unsaturated soils [ 56 ]. Brutsaert [ 56 ] extended the Biot’s theory to include unsaturated soils, while Berryman et al. [ 57 ] and Santos et al. [ 58 ,  59 – 60 ] further refined the governing equation for wave propagation in unsaturated media. Commonly used fundamental solutions for this case are obtained in the Laplace transformed domain by Hörmander’s method [ 61 ].

Anisotropic behavior is also frequently observed in natural soils as a result of geological processes such as sedimentation, leading to direction-dependent mechanical properties. This anisotropy affects wave propagation, resulting in elastic waves that propagate at a velocity dependent on direction, in contrast to isotropic cases. The investigation of anisotropic media originated in the nineteenth century with Love’s pioneering contributions [ 62 ]. Biot [ 63 ,  64 ] further formulated a theory for anisotropic porous media, presenting constitutive equations applicable to different frequency ranges. In general, anisotropy increases the number of elastic constants required in the constitutive law, resulting in numerical instability as well as computationally expensive, particularly in elastodynamic problems. To date, available 3D solutions for dynamic poroelasticity of anisotropic materials concentrate more on the transversely isotropic case [ 65 ,  66 ,  67 – 68 ].

Traditional PML may cause exponentially increasing backpropagation waves attributed to material anisotropy when simulating anisotropic media due to spurious reflections induced by discretization and zero-frequency singularities, resulting in significant computational errors [ 47 ]. Recent advancements by He and Li [ 20 ,  69 ] have extended the TLM by coupling it with the complex frequency-shifted perfectly matched layer (CFSPML), enhancing the method’s accuracy and efficiency for modeling wave propagation in anisotropic media.

sections.heading: Further cutting-edge advancement in wave propagation
paragraphs: Owing to the significant advancements in various technologies over the past decade, research into the problem of wave propagation has also experienced further innovation and development. These two types of problems can be categorized into solution and parameter inversion. Specifically, this involves exploring methods to obtain solutions more efficiently, as well as strategies for acquiring parameters that are more accurate, appropriate, and usable.

The application of deep learning-based model, exemplified by traditional artificial neural networks (NN) like back propagation NN, has been explored by some scholars in recent years [ 70 ,  71 – 72 ]. These studies have transformed physical problems, such as wave propagation processes, into data nonlinear fitting problems. In the field of mechanics, researchers frequently utilize experimental or computational data to train deep learning models, which can subsequently be employed for various research purposes, including simulations of dynamics behavior [ 71 ,  72 – 73 ]. Owing to its statistical scientific characteristics, such applications can be further extended to account for the uncertainty of wave propagation in actual soil condition [ 74 ,  75 ]. However, in most complex engineering and scientific systems encountered in real-world applications, data acquisition presents significant complexity and incurs substantial costs. The requirement for large volumes of data represents a critical limitation of deep learning, which may undermine the feasibility and robustness of this approach. In addition to their direct application in prediction of wave propagation, deep learning-based frameworks can also be employed to assist in accelerating computations, thereby enabling more efficient and rapid solutions to wave propagation [ 76 ]. In recent years, the incorporation of physical principles into deep learning frameworks has led to the development of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which integrate governing equations and domain knowledge directly into the learning process. Compared with traditional numerical solutions for partial differential equations. PINNs exhibit the characteristic of not requiring a mesh. This feature enables PINNs to address challenges that traditional numerical methods struggle with, such as problems in complex domains and inverse problem solving. The development of this framework was subsequently applied to address the problem of wave propagation in soils [ 77 ,  78 ,  79 – 80 ].

In the context of wave propagation problems, the application of new technologies remains largely in the exploratory phase. Regarding parameter inversion, numerous methods have been developed over the past decade and are gradually being implemented in the practical engineering. The inversion of site-specific soil parameters is typically carried out using surface wave testing methods, among which spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) and multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW) are the most widely adopted techniques. These technologies have found mainly extensive application in the field of earthquake engineering combined with the deep learning-based framework [ 81 ,  82 ,  83 ,  84 ,  85 – 86 ]. Through the application of wave propagation-based methods, parameters such as the damping ratio and shear wave velocity are inverted. This process facilitates the prediction of earthquakes and environmental vibrations, thereby enabling the acquisition of more accurate results [ 84 ,  85 – 86 ]. In addition, some computer vision-based technologies have also been developed and applied in wave propagation problems, such as the particle image velocimetry (PIV) method [ 87 ,  88 ]. This technique identifies the displacement field of sand for damping ratio inversion, thereby facilitating the analysis of material dynamic properties [ 88 ,  89 – 90 ]. However, its application remains predominantly confined to laboratory settings, posing significant challenges for implementation under in situ measurement conditions.

sections.heading: Modeling of ground vibrations induced by railway traffic
Excitation sources of train-induced vibrations
paragraphs: Train-induced vibrations are generated at the wheel–rail interface by wheelsets moving along the track. These vibrations can be categorized into two primary components based on their excitation mechanisms: the quasi-static component and the dynamic component. The quasi-static response arises from the constant wheel-axle loads moving on the rails. The repeated passage of wheelsets generates a series of characteristic peaks in the frequency spectrum. These peaks are primarily influenced by factors such as the train velocity and characteristic train dimensions, including the length of the carriages, the distance between wheelsets, and the bogie configuration [ 91 ,  92 – 93 ].

The dynamic component is induced by the interaction between the train and rails due to several different excitation mechanisms. The dominant mechanism involves the wheel and rail unevenness, which contribute significantly to the dynamic responses. The dynamic wheel–rail force due to the wheel and rail unevenness can be determined by a vehicle–track coupled dynamics model. The concept of vehicle-track coupled dynamics was first introduced by Zhai et al. [ 94 ,  95 – 96 ], as shown in Fig.  5 . Within the framework, the integrated vehicle subsystem and the track subsystem are coupled through a wheel–rail spatial coupling model that accounts for vibrations in vertical, lateral and torsional directions. Fig. 5 Vehicle–track coupled dynamics model proposed by Zhai [ 96 ]

In addition to wheel–rail unevenness, localized defects such as wheel flats, rail joints, and turnouts can also generate dynamic wheel–rail loads. Furthermore, parametric excitation due to the spatial variation of support stiffness, such as the discrete nature of sleeper and slab support, and the differential variation of the track and the subsoil, can also cause the dynamic wheel–rail load.

sections.heading: Analytical methods for train-induced ground vibrations
paragraphs: The foundation beam model is often used to simulate track structure of surface railways. Achenbach and Sun [ 98 ] summarized the early research on the foundation beam model under moving loads. Frýba et al. [ 99 ] proposed an analytical solution for the dynamic responses of beams, plates, and other structures on elastic and inelastic media under moving loads. Sheng et al. [ 100 ] further coupled the composite beam model to layered soils to calculate the dynamic responses under moving loads (Fig.  6 ). This model was further coupled with a multi-degree-of-freedom vehicle model to simulate the train-induced vibrations [ 91 ] and was validated through the site measurements [ 101 ]. Sadri et al. [ 102 ] proposed a robust periodic wheel/track model, incorporating a double ‘periodicity layer’ to investigate the influence of local and large-scale variation in the support stiffness. Fig. 6 a  Modeling of railway track on layered soils and  b  composite beam model for railway track. TI means transverse isotropic (both adapted from Sheng et al. [ 100 ])

For underground railway systems, the 2D embedded beam model was initially proposed to calculate ground vibrations from underground tunnels in a homogeneous half-space [ 103 ] and a layered half-space [ 104 ,  105 ]. However, the embedded beam model has two drawbacks. First, it assumes that the vibrations within the tunnel cross section are completely prohibited, resulting in significant errors above the first cut-on frequency of the tunnel structure [ 106 ]. Second, the model neglects wave propagation in the lateral direction.

To overcome these limitations, it is necessary to develop a prediction model that considers the 3D dynamic tunnel-soil interaction. The pipe-in-pipe (PiP) model, proposed by Forrest and Hunt [ 107 ], is the first 3D analytical approach to address these complexities. In this model, the foundation soil is represented as an infinitely thick cylinder with a full-space domain, while the tunnel lining is simulated by thin-walled cylindrical shell, as shown in Fig.  7 . The tunnel–soil system is assumed to be longitudinally invariant, resulting in an analytical solution in the frequency-wavenumber domain by using the Fourier transform (Eqs. ( 3 ) and ( 5 )). Forrest and Hunt [ 108 ], along with Hussein and Hunt [ 109 ,  110 ], subsequently improved the PiP model to analyze the dynamic responses under different types of track plates and different types of loads. In addition, Di et al. [ 111 ,  112 ] adapted the PiP model to account for the saturated and unsaturated characteristics of soils. By introducing the periodic-infinite structure theory, He et al. [ 113 ] proposed an improved 3D analytical method to calculate dynamic responses of a periodic jointed tunnel in soils, which overcomes the assumption that the shield-driving tunnels are homogeneous in the longitudinal direction. Hussein et al. [ 114 ] further introduced a fictitious force method to predict ground vibrations from a tunnel in a layered half-space based on the PiP model. As illustrated in Fig.  8 , this method consists of three primary steps. The displacement at the tunnel–soil interface is calculated in the first step by the PiP model for a full-space domain, as depicted in Fig.  8 a. In the second step, equivalent loads that produce the same tunnel displacements on the tunnel–soil interface are calculated through a fundamental solution for an elastic full space without tunnels, as shown in Fig.  8 b. Finally, the response of a multi-layered half-space is calculated by multiplying the responses due to those equivalent loads using a fundamental solution for a layered half-space. Although the fictitious force method provides a valuable approach for simulating ground vibrations from underground tunnels, it still overlooks the influence of the free surface and layer interfaces on the tunnel-soil interface response. This limitation results in reduced accuracy, particularly when the distance between the tunnel and the free surface or layer interfaces is less than twice the tunnel diameter [ 114 ]. Alsharo et al. [ 115 ] recently enhanced the engineering applicability of the PiP model by validating it against field measurements in desert geology (Qatar Metro). Their hybrid approach, which combined dynamic stiffness inversion with in situ monitoring, demonstrated the accuracy of this model in predicting vibration attenuation effects of rail pads under soft soil conditions. This study provided critical validation for the PiP model beyond conventional European/Asian geological cases [ 107 ,  108 ,  109 ,  110 ,  111 ,  112 ,  113 ,  114 ,  115 ,  116 ,  117 – 118 ]. Fig. 7 The diagram of PiP model [ 107 ] Fig. 8 The diagram of the fictitious force method:  a  full-space domain;  b  elastic full space;  c  multi-layered half space

Recently, He et al. [ 116 ,  117 ] proposed an innovative analytical method to predict vibrations from one or twin tunnel embedded in a layered half-space (Fig.  9 ). The tunnels are fully coupled with the multi-layered half-space via wave transformation and wave translation. As a result, this approach overcomes the limitation of the PiP model and ensures highly accuracy for the case of horizontally stratified soils. This model was further coupled with a vehicle-track model to provide an efficient prediction of ground vibrations generated by the passage of underground trains, with accuracy validated through site measurements [ 118 ]. Recently, He et al. [ 119 ] further extended this method to calculate dynamic responses from underwater tunnels in stratified soils, incorporating fluid–solid coupling. This extension has potential applications in evaluating the influence of train-induced hydroacoustic noise on aquatic ecosystems [ 120 ,  121 ]. Fig. 9 The model for  a  one single tunnel [ 116 ] and  b  twin tunnels [ 117 ] embedded in a multi-layered half-space

The aforementioned methods are computational efficient as they provide closed-form solution for the soil–structure dynamic interaction in a full-space, half-space, and even layered half-space in the frequency-wavenumber domain. However, analytical methods are less flexible with respect to geometrical variations. For example, the transition zone or embankment cannot be easily incorporated into the simulations of ground vibrations. Additionally, these models are typically limited to the circular tunnel and cannot accommodate multiple soil layers intersecting the tunnel. Each method presents distinct advantages and limitations. To assist practitioners in selecting appropriate approaches, Table  1  systematically compares the four primary methods discussed (composite beam, embedded beam, PiP, and wave decomposition method), summarizing their key characteristics, limitations, and recommended applications. This comparative analysis synthesizes findings from the theoretical developments and experimental validations presented throughout this section.
 Table 1 The comparison of four primary methods Method Composite beam model Embedded beam model PiP model Wave decomposition Assumptions Track-subgrade system as layered Timoshenko beams Stratified elastic soil (including half-space) Tunnel as Euler–Bernoulli beam 2D viscoelastic soil (plane strain) Vertical vibration only under cross-sectional constraints Infinite cylindrical thin shell (Flügge theory) Linear elastic theory/Biot’s theory) Periodic axle load excitation Wavefield decomposition (P/SV/SH waves) Multi-layered half-space superposition Wave transformation matrices Applicability scope Scenario: Surface railways Track: Straight alignment Soil: Layered (rigid/elastic base) Scenario: Shallow tunnels Tunnel: Circular/rectangular Soil: Layered (rigid/elastic base) Scenario: Deep buried tunnels Tunnel: Circular Soil: Layered (rigid/elastic base) Scenario: Complex geology/twin tunnels/underwater tunnel Tunnel: Circular; Arbitrary orientation Soil: Layered (rigid/elastic base) Strengths Full rail-pad-sleeper-ballast system modeling Direct input of sleeper spacing (Ls) for periodic excitation Analytical subcritical velocity solution Explicit Doppler shift via moving coordinates Full 3D tunnel-soil interaction Unified moving/harmonic load solution Grouting layer analysis Accurate interlayer reflections/refractions Dynamic interaction between tunnels analysis Arbitrary tunnel alignment capability Limitations Ignoring cross-sectional deformation of subgrade and embankment Ignoring cross-sectional deformation of tunnel Ignoring lateral wave propagation Ignoring free-surface and layer interface effects Failing in cross-sectional heterogeneity

While analytical methods provide efficient closed-form solutions, their accuracy may be compromised by spatial variability in soil properties and operational conditions (e.g., train speed). Recent studies by Tao et al. [ 122 ] demonstrated that soil inhomogeneity (modeled via log-normal random fields) and speed variations (uniform distribution) can induce significant stochasticity in vibration transmissions, with amplification probabilities reaching 7.6%–19.2% at 10 m from the track. This highlights the need to integrate probabilistic frameworks (e.g., Monte Carlo simulations) with deterministic analytical models for reliability-based design, particularly in geotechnically complex environments.

sections.heading: Numerical methods for train-induced ground vibrations
Numerical methods in the frequency domain
paragraphs: To account for the complex geometry of the ground and structures, numerical approaches in the frequency domain are frequently employed. The 2D and 3D finite element (FE) methods [ 123 ,  124 ,  125 – 126 ] have been commonly used to simulate ground vibrations induced by railway traffic. The 2D FE method offers high computational efficiency, while it ignores wave propagation in the longitudinal direction of tracks. The 3D FE method provides a more accurate representation, while suffering from reduced computational efficiency due to the large number of elements required. To bridge this gap, the 2.5D numerical approach has been introduced by assuming longitudinal invariance of the geometry and material properties, while allows for the simulation of 3D dynamic responses using a 2D mesh.

In addition, when FE method is used to simulate ground vibrations in a semi-infinite domain, it is crucial to properly treat the boundaries of the finite domain to prevent spurious reflections. Several boundary treatment methods have been developed such as the boundary element (BE), infinite element (IE) and perfectly matched layer (PML).

The BE method transforms the variable value problem into an integral equation using the reciprocal principle, which implicitly satisfies the radiation condition. Dominguez [ 127 ] derived the 3D boundary integral equation in the frequency domain. Savidis et al. [ 128 ] developed a 3D FE-BE model to simulate the dynamic interaction between the railway track and layered soils due to train loads. In this model, the BE method along with a fundamental solution for a layered half-space was introduced to simulate the unbounded soils. As a result, only mesh of 3D structures is required, significantly reducing the degrees of freedom. Andersen and Jones [ 129 ,  130 ] conducted a comparative study of dynamic responses calculated using the 3D and 2D FE-BE models. Their results revealed a striking disparity in computational efficiency: while the 2D model required only 5 s per frequency on a P4-2.8 GHz PC, the corresponding 3D model demanded over 2 h per frequency—more than 1000 times slower— due to the dense global stiffness matrices and axial wave propagation modeling [ 130 ]. To overcome this limitation, Sheng et al. [ 131 ,  132 ] first proposed the 2.5D coupled FE-BE method to compute ground vibrations from surface and underground railways. Their approach achieved computation time of approximately 15 min per frequency on a standard 3 GHz single-core PC, compared to an estimated 40 h per frequency. In addition, Hussein et al. [ 114 ] checked the computational efficiency of the extended PiP model. Their implementation required 5 s per frequency-wavenumber pair on a 2.4 GHz CPU), outperforming even the optimized 2.5D FE-BE model (100 s per pair on a hexa-core Xeon 2.66 GHz CPU). Crucially, all 2.5D methods maintained memory footprints below 1 GB RAM by leveraging dimensional reduction, whereas 3D models necessitated > 2 GB for global matrix storage, highlighting the dual advantage of efficiency and stability in reduced-dimensional approaches.

François et al. [ 133 ] further enhanced this method by introducing 2.5D Green’s functions for a layered half-space and a regularization procedure into the 2.5D BE method to avoid evaluating singular traction integrals and meshing at the ground surface and layer interfaces. He and Zhou [ 134 ,  135 ] further improved the 2.5D FE-BE method to simulate the dynamic interaction between saturated soils and structures. Jin et al. [ 136 ] coupled the 2.5D FE-BE model for a track-tunnel-ground system with a multi-body train model to compute ground vibrations induced by the running of underground trains, validating their results with site measurements.

As an alternative, the IE proposed by Ungless [ 137 ] can simulate wave propagation into the infinite domain. The IE is established by the shape function that combines a Lagrange interpolation function and an attenuation function. Li et al. [ 138 ] extended the application of the FE/IE method to vehicle-track-soil coupled systems. Through comparative analyses between 2 and 3D models, they demonstrated that the IE achieves a 30%–45% reduction in the number of degrees of freedom while maintaining accuracy in the 40–200 Hz range. A 2.5D FE-IE method was subsequently proposed by Yang and Hunt [ 139 ] to calculate ground vibrations induced by the passage of trains on embankments [ 140 ] and in underground tunnels [ 141 ].

Whereas the IE enforces radiation conditions through wave attenuation techniques, the Method of fundamental solutions (MFS) enforces satisfies these conditions by introducing strategically positioned virtual sources. When coupled with the FE method in 2.5D frameworks, MFS achieves high accuracy (< 2% error vs. FE-PML method [ 142 ]). However, its performance depends on the placement of virtual source, requiring careful tuning for complex geometries (e.g., sharp-edged tunnels [ 143 ]) and losing efficiency in highly heterogeneous media.

For broader applicability, the PML, introduced by Bérenger [ 144 ], uses a complex stretching function to ensure absorption of waves in all directions. 2D and 3D soil–structure dynamic interaction were subsequently investigated using a FE-PML method [ 145 ]. A 2.5D FE-PML method was next proposed to predict train-induced vibrations from underground tunnels [ 146 ,  147 ].

The 2.5D numerical methods offer high computational efficiency as only the 2D cross section need to be discretized. However, the assumption of longitudinal invariance makes the 2.5D methods incapable of accounting for parametric excitations due to periodic structural variations. To address this, a periodic FE-BE method was proposed to predict ground vibrations induced by railway traffic [ 4 ,  148 ]. This method utilizes the Floquet transform, which allows the 3D response to be determined on a single-bounded reference mesh. This approach was subsequently validated with site measurements from the Bakerloo line in London [ 149 ]. To capture longitudinal variation of structures efficiently, Germonpré et al. [ 150 ] proposed an innovative numerical method for multi-coupled periodic structures using the free-wave propagation theory [ 151 ]. This method was subsequently used to investigate dynamic responses in transition zones [ 152 ].

sections.heading: Numerical methods in the time domain
paragraphs: The methods in the time domain are essential for nonlinear behaviors involved in railway systems, such as the nonlinear wheel-rail contact relationship. Following the vehicle-track system dynamics [ 94 ,  95 – 96 ], it is necessary to account for the influence of the infrastructures under rails, such as the subgrade and tunnel. Recently, several models have been developed to simulate the dynamic interaction between the vehicle, track and subgrade [ 153 ,  154 ,  155 – 156 ]. Galvín et al. [ 153 ] developed a 3D multi-body FE-BE model in the time domain to calculate ground vibrations during the passage of high-speed trains. Similar work was also carried out by Feng et al. [ 157 ]. Connolly et al. [ 158 ] developed an explicit time-domain FE model that accounts for nonlinear excitation mechanisms to predict ground vibrations induced by surface railways. A significant advancement came from Xu et al. [ 159 ], who proposed a 3D vehicle-ballasted track-subgrade interaction model by coupling multi-body dynamics with FE-based substructures. This framework explicitly captured both lateral and vertical vibrations. Xu et al. [ 160 ] further enhanced this approach by developing a revolutionary multiscale matrix assembly strategy that hybridizes implicit integration with matrix bandwidth optimization techniques. This strategy led to a 62% reduction in computational time for longitudinal non-uniform track systems. Recently, Li and Xu [ 161 ] further advanced the framework by incorporating Green’s function-based formulations with cyclic iterative calculations to enhance efficiency in modeling soil–track interactions. However, these models neglect longitudinal variations in the railway track. Shan et al. [ 156 ,  162 ] developed a vehicle-track-subgrade-ground interaction model for bridge–embankment transition zones, revealing the dynamic response characteristics due to stiffness changes in these transition areas.

Numerous models have also been developed in the time domain to compute soil vibrations from underground tunnels [ 125 ,  163 ]. However, simulating soils in a semi-infinite domain using the FE method results in substantial computational demands. An alternative time-domain model was also proposed to simulate the vehicle-track-tunnel dynamic interaction [ 159 ,  164 ]. In those models, the soils were simulated as a series of supported springs, neglecting wave propagation in the ground. Xu and Zhai [ 165 ] addressed this limitation by coupling finite and infinite elements to explicitly model soil wave propagation. A semi-analytical model was first developed using the substructure method [ 166 ], followed by a semi-analytical FE approach incorporating Fourier series to simulate wave propagation in the soil, thereby reducing the degrees of freedom and improving computational efficiency. This method was subsequently improved by Yang et al. [ 167 ] to the case of curved tunnels.

sections.heading: Modeling of building vibrations induced by railway traffic
paragraphs: Building upon the modeling of railway-induced ground vibrations, increasing attention has been directed toward predicting building vibrations caused by railway traffic. This section presents a comprehensive review of prediction methods in the frequency and time domains as well as the time–frequency hybrid methods for assessing train-induced vibrations in buildings.

sections.heading: Prediction methods in the frequency domain
paragraphs: The prediction of train-induced vibrations involves three primary subsystems: the vibration source, including the vehicle–track system; the propagation path, comprising the infrastructures and underlying soils; and the receiver, which is the building. The coupling of these subsystems is a crucial aspect for accurately assessing train-induced environmental vibrations. Numerous studies have addressed these coupling issues, with the sub-structuring approach being one of the most efficient methods for accounting for the interaction between each subsystem. Lopes et al. [ 168 ] proposed a numerical model to predict building vibrations from underground railway traffic via the sub-structuring approach. As shown in Fig.  10 , the multi-rigid body approach is used to simulate train dynamics, while a 2.5D FE-PML and 3D FE approaches are applied to model the track-tunnel-ground system and building vibrations in this approach. This model was further validated by comparing with the site measurements [ 169 ]. A similar model was proposed by Fiala et al. [ 170 ] to predict building vibrations and structure-borne noise from surface railway traffic. Fig. 10 Numerical model proposed by Lopes et al. [ 168 ] to predict building vibrations from underground railway traffic via the sub-structuring approach

Analytical and semi-analytical models were also proposed to calculate train-induced building vibrations as an efficient way. Hussein et al. [ 171 ] developed a sub-structuring method where the tunnel-soil dynamic interaction was modeled using the PiP method and building vibrations were modeled with a 2D frame model of beam elements. He et al. [ 172 ] developed an analytical model for dynamic responses of buildings with shallow foundations generated by underground railway traffic. As shown in Fig.  11 , the wave decomposition method [ 116 ,  117 ] was introduced to simulate wave propagation in tunnels and layered soils more accuracy in this model. In addition, a 3D frame model consisting of plates and rods, based on the dynamic stiffness method, was proposed to simulate dynamic responses of buildings with shallow foundation. Li et al. [ 173 ] further improved this model to predict train-induced building vibrations supported by pile foundations, as shown in Fig.  12 . An impedance model combined the building structure and pile foundation was introduced here, resulting in higher computational efficiency [ 174 ,  175 ]. The accuracy of this model is validated by comparing with the site measurements for building vibrations located near the metro tunnel in Guangzhou, China. Fig. 11 Analytical model for dynamic responses of buildings with shallow foundation generated by underground railway traffic [ 172 ] Fig. 12 Analytical model for dynamic responses of buildings with pile foundation generated by underground railway traffic [ 173 ]

The sub-structuring approach, however, excludes secondary coupling effects, such as the influence of the building structure on the response of the track and vehicle. To examine the influence of the source-receiver interaction, Coulier et al. [ 176 ] used a 2.5D FE-BE method to simulate the track (tunnel)-ground-building system. By assuming that the building to be a longitudinally invariant structure, the fully coupling between the train-track system and the building was considered. The results demonstrate that the interaction between the building and tunnel mainly affects the power flow distribution if their distance is smaller than the dilatational wavelength in soils. In addition, the interaction effects for a railway track at grade are observed if the track-building distance is smaller than six times Rayleigh wavelength. Edirisinghe and Talbot [ 177 ] further developed a robust model to calculate building vibrations that considered the source(tunnels)-receiver (piled foundation) interaction. The iterative wave-scattering method was applied to tunnel subsystem and the piled foundation subsystem to account for their dynamic interaction. However, this procedure requires meshing the tunnels and piles, which significantly increases computational efforts. Based on this fully coupled model, Edirisinghe and Talbot [ 178 ] further investigated the influence of four types of soil–structure interaction (soil–pile interaction, pile–soil–pile interaction, tunnel–soil–foundation interaction, and soil–foundation–building interaction, illustrated in Fig.  13 , in a tunnel–soil–foundation–building system under various building locations, relative to the tunnel, pile lengths and foundation configurations. This study provided a guideline for the simplified modeling of train-induced building vibrations. Another fully coupled approach for predicting the building vibrations from railway traffic was proposed by Bucinskas et al. [ 179 ]. In this approach, the railway train moving on the track is modeling in a moving frame of reference, while the interacting via the soil with the building is formulated in a fixed frame of reference. A mixed frame of reference formulation is introduced to couple the two frames of reference, thereby obtaining a fully coupled solution for the entire system. Fig. 13 The influence of soil–structure interaction in a tunnel–foundation–building system:  a  free-field responses due to the wave-fields from the underground railway tunnel;  b  foundation responses involving soil–pile interaction, pile–soil–pile interaction and tunnel–soil–foundation interaction; and  c  building responses involving soil–foundation–building interaction [ 178 ]

sections.heading: Prediction methods in the time-domain and time–frequency hybrid methods
paragraphs: Prediction methods in the time-domain and time–frequency hybrid methods provide alternative approaches. 2D and 3D numerical methods [ 123 ,  180 ] have been proposed to predict building vibrations generated by underground and surface railway traffic. These methods require spatial discretization and time step variations, leading to numerous degrees of freedom. Additionally, the iterative step sizes differ across subsystems, making time-domain prediction methods computationally inefficient. To avoid the low computational efficiency associated with the methods in the time domain, the hybrid approach in both time and frequency domain was developed. Yang et al. [ 181 ] proposed a two-step numerical method to predict the building vibrations induced by underground railways. As shown in Fig.  14 , the train-track coupled dynamic model [ 93 ,  94 ,  95 – 96 ] is used to determine the rail supporting forces in the time domain, while a 3D FE method for the track-tunnel-ground-building system is developed to calculate the building vibrations under the rail supporting forces in the frequency domain. Connolly et al. [ 182 ] also presented a hybrid time–frequency domain method to predict train-induced vibrations in buildings. Similarly, Qiu et al. [ 183 ] developed a numerical model combining train-track-slab coupling dynamics in the time domain with track structure-building-soil finite element analysis. In this approach, a FE model for the vehicle-track-soil system in the time domain is used to calculate the force density due to wheel-rail-defect interaction, while a 2.5D FE-BE method is subsequently employed to determine the track-soil transfer function in the frequency domain. The soil–building interaction is finally calculated by using the 3D FE method in the time domain. López-Mendoza et al. [ 184 ] assessed the train-induced building vibration with a wide range of footing shapes by using the hybrid time–frequency method. Qu et al. [ 185 ] also proposed a hybrid approach based on the vehicle-track coupled dynamics theory in the time domain, a 2.5D FE model for the track-tunnel-ground system, and a FE model for building vibrations. The vibrations of a hospital close to a new subway line were evaluated by using this hybrid approach. Fig. 14 Two-step numerical method for predicting the building vibrations induced by underground railways in the time domain [ 181 ]

sections.heading: Empirical and semi-empirical methods
paragraphs: As an alternative to purely numerical approaches, empirical methods offer an efficient means for predicting train-induced vibrations. The empirical procedure proposed by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) and the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) of the U.S. Department of Transportation [ 186 ,  187 ] has been adopted in many countries. This method relies on a chain attenuation formula, which characterizes both the source and the propagation path [ 188 ,  189 ]. The source in this empirical method is defined as a line force density, representing a series of point force distributed along the railway line. The line force density can be determined by measuring vibrations at a fixed distance from the track during the passage of trains. Vibration propagation is described by the transfer function, which represents the relationship between a line force density of unit amplitude and the vibration velocity observed at a given distance from the track. This transfer function can be obtained through measurements such as hammering or dropped-weight tests. In addition, based on the Channel Tunnel Rail Link project in the UK, Hood et al. [ 190 ] proposed a similar empirical method that accounts prediction uncertainty. Kuppelwieser and Ziegler [ 191 ] and Madshus [ 192 ] applied this approach in Switzerland and Scandinavia, respectively. Rossi and Nicolini [ 193 ] proposed a simplified model to quickly predict soil vibration velocity levels induced by high-speed trains, including decibel levels and root mean squared values.

At the soil layer propagation level, a critical limitation of empirical formulas lies in their inability to account for stratified soil conditions. Stratified soil layers are typically be simplified to a semi-infinite space, and the degree of influence of soil stiffness will be further analyzed and compared. In the empirical correction of FRA/FTA, two cases were considered: efficient propagation soils and wave transmission through rock layers. A conservative estimation approach recommends applying a 10 dB adjustment for efficient propagation to evaluate the maximum potential vibration impact.

Beyond wave propagation characteristics, soil type also significantly influences coupling loss at the soil–structure interface, which governs the degree of vibration transfer into built infrastructure. The SILVARSTAR project [ 194 ] categorized soils into soft, medium, and hard types based on the specific threshold values of transverse wave velocity outlined in Eurocode 8 [ 195 ]. This classification further facilitated the provision of precise correction factors for different one-third octave bands. Chinese Standard HJ 453-2018 [ 196 ] categorizes soils into four types according to the shear wave velocity, assigning distinct correction coefficients accordingly. Similarly, the consideration of soil stratification is essential for calculating the equivalent shear wave velocity of soils. However, in both standards, soil stratification is often approximated through an equivalent shear wave velocity, without explicitly modeling the effects of interlayer wave reflection and refraction.

As such, although existing empirical approaches provide practical correction frameworks, they tend to adopt conservative estimates and do not fully capture the complexity of wave propagation in stratified soils. The authors posit that using equivalent shear wave velocity to distinguish between soft and hard soils remains a reasonable approximation for empirical modeling. The applicability of such models is often constrained by specific geological settings, such as soils with progressively increasing stiffness with depth (e.g., coastal soft soils in Shanghai, China) or surface-exposed stiff strata (e.g., certain European regions). To improve the generalizability and predictive accuracy of empirical models, it is recommended to restructure existing databases based on representative site conditions and to develop stratification-sensitive correction factors tailored to different wave propagation scenarios.

However, the empirical methods are limited to cases where the track and soil characteristics are available. This limitation can be addressed by integrating numerical methods into empirical techniques, leading to the development of hybrid numerical/experimental methods. Verbraken et al. [ 197 ] proposed a hybrid model to predict railway-induced vibrations, where the 2.5D FE-BE method offers flexibility in modeling different train-track systems, while the empirical method provides an accurate assessment of vibration propagation through soils. Kuo et al. [ 198 ,  199 ] presented a hybrid method combining recorded data and numerical predictions, in line with the FRA’s definitions. In a similar concept, Ma and Liu [ 3 ] proposed a two-position calibration method, where in situ measurements are used to calibrate both the input and output of numerical models in the time domain. Liu et al. [ 200 ] combined the vibration transmission data, obtained through in situ measurements inside and outside a building, with a numerical model to assess the effects of metro-induced vibrations on sensitive equipment.

Beyond conventional approaches, there has been growing interest in leveraging machine learning techniques to develop intelligent prediction systems based on existing data. Recent advancements in data-driven modeling have significantly enhanced predictive capabilities. Liang et al. [ 201 ] developed a Bayesian neural network (BNN) that not only predicts vibration levels but also quantifies prediction uncertainty through probability distributions. Kedia et al. [ 202 ] demonstrated the superiority of PSO-ANN hybrid models over traditional methods in Delhi Metro case studies, particularly in handling heterogeneous soil conditions. Paneiro et al. [ 203 ] proposed multiple linear regression models to predict vibration amplitudes generated by railway traffic. Connolly et al. [ 70 ,  71 ] proposed a neural network-based model, called Scope rail, to assess vibrations induced by the operation of high-speed railway trains. Paneiro et al. [ 72 ] introduced an artificial neural network (ANN) approach to predict ground vibrations induced by railway traffic. Liang et al. [ 74 ] proposed a probabilistic model using a Bayesian neural network, which provides a probability distribution for prediction results to quantify uncertainty. A case study based on the site measurements from Beijing was performed to examine the performance of the proposed model. Li et al. [ 204 ] combined the Bayesian neural network with a numerical model for predict vibrations in buildings, incorporating the coupling loss of soils and building structures. Tu et al. [ 73 ] proposed a prediction approach for building vibrations from subway traffic, in which both numerical results and site measurements were used for training in machine learning.

Despite their potential, these data-driven methods face challenges, particularly due to the limited availability of high-quality site measurements, which can lead to insufficient training data for machine learning models. To mitigate these issues, a model that combines the physical-based and data-driven methods may provide a promising solution. Galvín et al. [ 205 ] employed an artificial neural network to adjust the Green’s function for soils, eliminating the need for mechanical modeling of soil–track dynamic interaction, which significantly reduces computational time. Wang et al. [ 206 ] recently proposed a hybrid model to predict environmental vibrations induced by subway traffic by combining physical-numerical and deep learning methods. In this approach, the numerical method was used to remove outlier data, thus enhancing the accuracy of the input data for the data-driven model. Notably, Liang and Liu [ 207 ] achieved 98.3% recognition accuracy for vibration patterns using CNN-LSTM (long short-term memory) hybrid models with continuous wavelet transforms, demonstrating the potential of deep learning in handling complex vibration signals.

sections.heading: Discussion on areas for future research
paragraphs: Environmental issues related to train-induced vibrations from railway traffic are becoming increasingly significant. The developed prediction methods have provided a systematic understanding of vibration generation and propagation characteristics, aiding in the design of effective mitigation measures. However, several unresolved issues remain that require further investigation.

(1)  Wave propagation in inhomogeneous soils : Various analytical and numerical methods have been proposed to simulate soil dynamics and soil–structure dynamic interaction in full-space, half-space and layered half-space domains. However, the natural inhomogeneity of soils, characterized by variations in mineral composition, stress history, moisture content, and density, results in both geometric variations among soil layers and spatial variability of soil properties. Site measurements have illustrated that the soil inhomogeneity has a significant influence on train-induced ground vibrations [ 149 ]. Recently, a semi-analytical approach was developed to investigate the effect of irregular layering on ground vibrations from underground tunnels [ 208 ,  209 ]. This method incorporates virtual horizontal interfaces and boundary integral equations into the wave decomposition technique [ 116 ], enabling the simulation of arbitrarily shaped interfaces with only irregular portions discretized. However, the approach is currently limited to 2D problems, and further research is needed to extend it to general 3D cases. In addition, highly efficient numerical methods are required to simulate wave propagation soil dynamics and soil–structure dynamic interaction that account for the soil inhomogeneity.

(2)  Uncertainty in prediction of train-induced vibrations : Current methods primarily focus on deterministic predictions of train-induced vibrations. However, the input parameters involving in these calculations are subject to random uncertainties. For instance, the uncertainty in wheel/rail loads arises from variations in vehicle types, changes in wheel-rail roughness over time and space, and spatial variability in track stiffness. In addition, the spatial variability of soil properties contributes significantly to the uncertainty of environmental vibrations. To quantify these uncertainties in train-induced vibrations, Monte Carlo simulations (MCS) with a large number of realizations are typically required, leading to slow convergence and extensive time consumption. In addition to developing more high-efficient physical models, the model order reduction technique [ 209 ,  210 – 211 ] may provide a promising avenue for addressing uncertainty problems. This is particularly useful for cases involving a large number of realizations.

(3)  Prediction models combining physics-based principles with data-driven methods : Machine learning and deep learning algorithms offer significant advantages in deep data mining and processing complex nonlinear relationships, making them well-suited for data-driven prediction methods. Various studies have been carried out to develop prediction models based on machine learning and deep learning algorithms [ 203 ,  204 ,  205 – 206 ]. However, due to limited availability and varied formats of site-measurements, the reliability of prediction models based solely on machine or deep learning techniques remains questionable. To enhance model accuracy, it is crucial to conduct on-site measurements and share the original data. With large datasets, machine learning models can achieve high reliability and broad applicability. In addition, prediction models combining physics-based principles with data-driven methods may offer a promising solution. The incorporation of physical laws could mitigate the limitations imposed by limited site measurements of train-induced vibrations. In particular, physics-informed neural networks [ 80 ,  212 ] represent a potentially effective approach for integrating physical insights into data-driven prediction models.

Accurate prediction of train-induced vibrations represents a critical nexus between railway engineering advancement and environmental stewardship. This review highlights three fundamental challenges that need to be addressed: inhomogeneous soil modeling, uncertainty quantification, and physics-data fusion. Dealing with these challenges is essential as it can transform vibration analysis from a reactive mitigation tool to a proactive design instrument.

Addressing these issues enables several key advancements. First, track systems can be designed to align with site-specific geotechnical conditions, minimizing unnecessary material use and improving efficiency. Second, the deployment of uncertainty-aware digital twins facilitates the optimized design of vibration mitigation measures—such as barriers—thereby enhancing infrastructure durability and extending service life. Third, it allows for low-emission railway planning by predictively mapping environmental impacts. These capabilities directly contribute to UN SDG targets on sustainable transport infrastructure (9.1) and urban environmental management (11.6).

Moving forward, the integration of domain-embedded machine learning with next-generation soil characterization technologies is crucial. This combination promises to unlock vibration prediction models that not only safeguard ecosystems but also accelerate the transition to climate-resilient rail networks. In this way, vibration control is elevated from a mere technical afterthought to a cornerstone strategy. This strategy is key to redefining railways as sustainable mobility backbones for the twenty-first century.
